claims.text: Nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films and nanoribbons have elevated interface strain due to their low-dimensional geometry and substrate interactions.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type nanostructures have elevated defect densities arising from deposition or patterning.
Interface strain and defects enhance magnetic domain-wall pinning.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning broadens and slows the magnetic phase transition during low-field cycling.
Transition broadening and slowing reduce the effective magnetocaloric entropy change relative to bulk forms.
Transition broadening and slowing increase magnetic hysteresis relative to bulk forms.
Annealing at approximately 300–400 °C can partially relieve substrate-induced strain.
Annealing at approximately 300–400 °C can reduce defect density without changing the overall phase composition or causing significant phase coarsening.
Substrate- and processing-induced strain creates inhomogeneous magnetic anisotropy.
Inhomogeneous magnetic anisotropy and domain-wall pinning hinder continuous and reversible magnetization changes during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Relieving strain through annealing should reduce domain-wall pinning.
Reduced pinning should produce a sharper magnetic transition.
Reduced pinning should increase the magnetocaloric response.
Heat-transfer limitations associated with the nanoscale geometry constrain magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
Limited heat-transfer rates may accentuate hysteretic behavior.
Compared with as-deposited controls, annealed samples should exhibit narrower hysteresis loops.
Compared with as-deposited controls, annealed samples should exhibit a larger magnetocaloric entropy change.
Post-annealing effective cooling capacity should improve under otherwise identical low-field cycling conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to films thinner than 100 nm or nanoribbons narrower than approximately 500 nm.
The proposed operating regime is below 100 mT, near the intrinsic magnetic transition temperature, and at ambient pressure.
